questions.stem: Approximately how long is the menstrual cycle?
questions.explanation: The menstrual cycle is approximately 28 days long, though it can vary between 21-35 days. It involves a repeating sequence of events controlled by four main hormones: FSH, LH, oestrogen, and progesterone.

questions.stem: What event occurs on approximately day 14 of the menstrual cycle?

options.text: Ovulation (an egg is released from the ovary)
The uterus lining starts to build up

questions.explanation: Ovulation occurs around day 14, when a mature egg is released from the ovary. This is triggered by a surge in LH (luteinising hormone). Ovulation is the most fertile time in the cycle.

questions.stem: What is the role of FSH in the menstrual cycle?

options.text: It stimulates follicle development in the ovary

questions.explanation: FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) is produced by the pituitary gland and stimulates the development of follicles in the ovary. Each follicle contains an egg. FSH also stimulates the follicle to produce oestrogen.

questions.stem: Which hormone is responsible for maintaining the uterus lining after ovulation?
questions.explanation: Progesterone is produced by the corpus luteum (the remains of the follicle after ovulation) and maintains the thick uterus lining. If pregnancy does not occur, progesterone levels drop, and the lining breaks down causing menstruation.

questions.stem: What triggers the surge in LH that causes ovulation?

options.text: High levels of oestrogen produced by the mature follicle

questions.explanation: As the follicle matures, it produces increasing levels of oestrogen. When oestrogen reaches a high enough level, it triggers a positive feedback effect on the pituitary gland, causing a sudden surge of LH which triggers ovulation.

questions.stem: Where is oestrogen produced during the menstrual cycle?
questions.explanation: Oestrogen is produced by the developing follicle in the ovaries. It causes the uterus lining to thicken and repair after menstruation, and at high levels triggers the LH surge that causes ovulation.

options.text: A surge of LH from the pituitary gland
A drop in progesterone levels when the corpus luteum breaks down

questions.explanation: If no pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum degenerates and stops producing progesterone. Without progesterone to maintain it, the thick uterus lining breaks down and is shed, causing menstruation (the period).
